segments.title: Song and Yuan Buddhist art at Kyoto National Museum
segments.summary: A non-specialist response to Song and Yuan Buddhist painting focuses on expressive figures, tapestries, and ceramics.
segments.body: The main exhibition at the Kyoto National Museum was closed during this visit, leaving an exhibition of Song and Yuan Buddhist painting as the day's focus. The video introduces the exhibition and then gives a reaction afterwards, since filming inside was expected to be restricted. The response is explicitly non-specialist and concentrates on the visual impact of the works, without attempting a technical account of Song or Yuan art. Strong lines and facial expressions make the figures seem to leap from the page. The tapestries and ceramics also draw admiration for their craftsmanship.

evidence.note: He introduces the Song and Yuan Buddhist art exhibition and describes the expressive figures, textiles, and ceramics that impressed him.

segments.title: Lacquered wooden Buddhas seen through family carpentry
segments.summary: A family background in carpentry brings the chisel work, fine detail, shaping, and bending of lacquered wooden Buddhas into focus.
segments.body: The lacquered wooden Buddhas in the museum's lower levels are the part of the visit that feels most familiar. The family background described here includes a father and grandfather who both did a great deal of carpentry and furniture making. That familiarity with wood provides more vocabulary for appreciating these sculptures than for the paintings. Attention turns to the chisel work, fine detail, bending, shaping, and forming of the wood. The appreciation centres on the skill visible in the wooden figures; no specific carving technique or date is identified.

evidence.note: He connects the lacquered wooden Buddha figures with family carpentry experience and names their chisel work, fine detail, bending, and shaping.
